Minimum Risk Point Estimation of the Coefficient of Variation

Source: R/seq_mr_cv.R
seq_mr_cv.Rd

Given the data collected so far, evaluates the purely sequential minimum risk point estimation (MRPE) stopping rule of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) for the population coefficient of variation \(\kappa = \sigma / \mu\). The procedure is for a study in which each observation costs money and a less accurate estimate also has a cost: it stops sampling when the estimated total of the two is as small as it can be. It targets a risk, not a confidence interval, so there is no confidence level.

Usage

seq_mr_cv(
  x,
  A,
  c,
  gamma = 0.49,
  variance = c("corrected", "published"),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector: the observations collected so far, at least four. The coefficient of variation is meaningful for a quantity measured on a ratio scale with a positive mean (the article assumes nonnegative data); it is not meaningful for centered or standardized scores or for differences, whose mean can be zero.

A

The loss constant: the price of one unit of squared estimation error, in the same currency as c. The article builds it as the amount one is willing to pay to estimate the coefficient of variation to within \(\epsilon\), divided by \(\epsilon^2\) (for example \(1000 / 0.05^2 = 400000\)). A single positive number.

c

The cost of sampling one observation. A single positive number.

gamma

The tuning constant of the correction term, strictly between 0 and 1/2; default 0.49. Use the same value as in seq_mr_cv_pilot.

variance

Which estimator of the asymptotic variance \(\xi^2\) to use: "corrected" (the default), the consistent estimator of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018); or "published", Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016), for reproducing that article. See Details.

na.rm

Should missing values be removed before the computation? TRUE (the default) removes them; FALSE stops with an error if any are present.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") with columns term and value and one row for each of

cv

the sample coefficient of variation, \(s_n / \bar{X}_n\);

risk

the estimated risk at the current sample size, \(A\,\hat{\xi}_n^2 / n + c\,n\);

xi_squared

the variance estimate \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\) from the estimator chosen by variance, bounded below by \(n^{-3}\) (it equals \(n^{-3}\) when the variance cannot be estimated);

optimal_n

the criterion sample size, rounded up: the stopping rule is met exactly when current_n is at least optimal_n. When the variance cannot be estimated it is at least current_n + 1;

current_n

the number of observations supplied.

Attributes: is_satisfied (whether to stop sampling: TRUE or FALSE, never NA), current_n, criterion_n (equal to optimal_n), method, loss_A, cost_c, gamma, variance (the estimator used), variance_unusable, and notes (a character vector, printed under the result). The attribute variance_unusable is TRUE when the variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite (see Details). conf_level and width are NULL. When the sample mean is not positive, cv, risk, xi_squared, optimal_n, and criterion_n are NA. See smsd_check_methods for the print, summary, and conversion methods.

Details

The function does not collect data or keep state. Call seq_mr_cv_pilot for the starting sample size, collect that many observations, then call seq_mr_cv() after each new observation (or batch) until attr(out, "is_satisfied") is TRUE.

The risk and the stopping rule. The loss of estimating \(\kappa\) by the sample coefficient of variation \(k_n = s_n / \bar{X}_n\) from \(n\) observations is the squared error priced at \(A\) plus the sampling cost, and its expectation is the risk \(R_n(\kappa) = A\,E[(k_n - \kappa)^2] + c\,n\) (Equation 11 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley, 2016). For samples that are not too small this is approximately \(A\,\xi^2 / n + c\,n\) (their Equation 14), where \(\xi^2\) is the asymptotic variance of \(\sqrt{n}\,(k_n - \kappa)\). The approximate risk is smallest at \(n_c = (A/c)^{1/2}\,\xi\) (their Equation 15), where it equals \(2 c\, n_c\) (their Equation 16). Because \(\xi\) is unknown, the purely sequential rule (their Equation 23) stops at the first \(n \ge m\) with $$n^2 \ge \frac{A}{c}\left(\hat{\xi}_n^2 + n^{-2\gamma}\right),$$ where \(m\) is the pilot size, \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\) estimates \(\xi^2\) from the data, and \(n^{-2\gamma}\) with \(0 < \gamma < 1/2\) keeps the rule from stopping too early while the estimate is still noisy. The reported optimal_n is the same criterion on the scale of \(n\), \(\lceil (A/c)^{1/2} (\hat{\xi}_n^2 + n^{-2\gamma})^{1/2} \rceil\), and the reported risk is \(A\,\hat{\xi}_n^2 / n + c\,n\). The coefficient of variation and the estimate \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\) are ratios in which the units of the data cancel, so the result is the same whatever the units (centimeters or meters, dollars or thousands of dollars), up to rounding error.

Two variance estimators. The argument variance chooses \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\).

  • "corrected" (the default; use this one) is the estimator of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Equations 31 and 32), the sample version of the asymptotic variance in their Equation 30, $$\xi^2 = \frac{\mu_4}{4\mu^2\sigma^2} - \frac{\sigma^2}{4\mu^2} - \frac{\mu_3}{\mu^3} + \frac{\sigma^4}{\mu^4},$$ where \(\mu_3\) and \(\mu_4\) are the third and fourth central moments. It is consistent for any population with a positive mean and a finite fourth moment, and it is the estimator seq_aipe_cv uses.

  • "published" is Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016), the sample version of their Equation 9, $$\frac{\mu_4}{4\mu^4} + \frac{\sigma^4}{4\mu^4} - \frac{\mu_3}{\mu^3} + \frac{\sigma^2}{2\mu^2}.$$ It is offered so that the article's worked example and tables, and the results of mr_cv in DMAR and mr.cv() in MBESS, can be reproduced.

The two expressions differ by \(\frac{1}{4}\kappa^2 (1 - \kappa^2)(\mu_4/\sigma^4 - 3)\). They are therefore equal for a normal population, and for any population with no excess kurtosis, and they differ otherwise. For gamma data with \(\kappa = 0.8\), for example, \(n\) times the mean squared error of \(k_n\) at \(n = 400\) was 0.516 in a simulation of 200,000 samples (standard error 0.002); the corrected expression gives 0.525 and the published one 0.304. In the full procedure for that population (\(A\) = 5,000,000, \(c\) = 10; 5,000 replications) the risk is smallest at 512 observations; the mean final sample size was 479 with the corrected estimator and about 374 with the published one (the article's Table 1 reports 374.0). The derivation, with code that a reader can run, is in the file cv_variance_note.md installed with the package (system.file("cv_variance_note.md", package = "SMSD")). Both estimators use the unbiased estimators of \(\mu_3\) and \(\mu_4\) (Equations 20 and 21 of the 2016 article), and a positive estimate from either is bounded below by \(n^{-3}\), as in Equation 31 of the 2018 article (Equation 22 of the 2016 article has no such bound; the package applies it to the published estimator as well).

When the variance cannot be estimated. If the variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite (every observation so far is the same, or the same to ten significant digits, or the sample gives a negative estimate), the function reports the stopping rule as not met, sets attr(out, "variance_unusable") to TRUE, and adds a note; see smsd_check_methods. This is a deliberate departure from the article's rule, which read literally would stop at once on such an estimate. A positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe, so a small coefficient of variation does not by itself make an estimate unusable.

What the departure costs depends on how often the estimate is negative. For normal data that is seldom. With a coefficient of variation of 0.10, \(A\) = 400, and \(c\) = 1 (a pilot size of 8), the mean final sample size in 2,000 simulated runs was 8.05, where the rule as printed, with the bound in place of a negative estimate, gave 8.00. It is frequent for a quantity that takes only two or three distinct values and has a small coefficient of variation: the asymptotic variance of such a population is close to zero (it is \(\kappa^4\) for two equally likely values), the default estimate is a difference of terms that nearly cancel, and it is negative at many stages in a row. For observations equal to 9 or 11 with equal probability (\(\kappa\) = 0.10) and the same constants, the rule as printed stopped at 8 in every one of 2,000 runs. This function reports the rule as met at 8 with probability exactly one half (when 1, 2, 5, 6, or 7 of the 8 observations are 11) and keeps sampling otherwise: in the same 2,000 runs it stopped at 8 in 48.5 percent, the mean final sample size was 25, the 90th percentile 51, the 99th percentile 244, and the largest 693. (With variance = "published" the mean was 8.01, because Equation 22 seldom turns negative for such data; for this population, however, its large sample value is about fifty times the asymptotic variance.) If the quantity you measure takes very few distinct values, decide on a largest sample size before sampling begins.

Agreement with mr_cv() in DMAR. With variance = "published" this function and mr_cv apply the same rule to the same number whenever Equation 22 is at least \(n^{-3}\), as it is in the article's example. mr_cv() applies Equation 22 as printed, with no lower bound, so for a smaller value, which occurs in small samples, the two can differ, in two ways.

  • Equation 22 is zero or negative. This function reports the rule as not met; mr_cv() uses the value and can stop. In 4,000 samples of 8 observations from a lognormal population (log scale standard deviation 1, \(A\) = 400, \(c\) = 1), Equation 22 was zero or negative in 223 (5.6 percent), and mr_cv() stopped on each of them.

  • Equation 22 is positive but below \(n^{-3}\). This function uses \(n^{-3}\) in its place, so its risk row is the larger of the two, and so is its criterion: the decisions differ when \(n^2\) lies between \((A/c)(V_n^2 + n^{-2\gamma})\) and \((A/c)(n^{-3} + n^{-2\gamma})\), with \(V_n^2\) for Equation 22. The band is narrow (with the default \(\gamma\), at most 1.5 percent of \(n^2\) at \(n\) = 8 and 0.6 percent at \(n\) = 13), but when \(A/c\) puts \(n^2\) inside it the two functions disagree for every sample with so small an estimate. For the eight heights 168.2, 171.9, 166.4, 173.5, 170.8, 169.1, 174.6, and 167.3 (Equation 22 is 0.00015, and \(8^{-3}\) is 0.00195) with \(c\) = 1, both functions report the rule as met at \(A\) = 400 and as not met at \(A\) = 500. At \(A\) = 485, mr_cv() reports it as met (63.3 against \(n^2\) = 64) and this function as not met (64.1 against 64). In 4,000 samples of 8 normal observations with a coefficient of variation of 0.02, the two decisions were the same in every sample at \(A\) = 400 and different in every sample at \(A\) = 485.

When the mean is not positive. If the sample mean is zero or negative, the coefficient of variation is not estimable: the estimate, risk, variance, and criterion are NA, the rule is reported as not met, and a note says why. A mean that differs from zero only by rounding error (no larger than about 2e-15 times the largest absolute observation, as for centered or standardized scores) is treated as zero, whatever its sign. A positive mean that is very close to zero gives a very large coefficient of variation, and the function stops with an error if the criterion that follows is too large to represent.

What to expect. The article proves that the expected final sample size and the risk approach their optimal values as \(A/c\) grows; at practical sizes the agreement is approximate. In simulations of the default procedure with \(A\) = 5,000,000 and \(c\) = 10 (5,000 replications each), the ratio of the mean final sample size to \(n_c\) was 1.18 for normal and for gamma data with \(\kappa = 0.2\) (there \(n_c\) is near the pilot size, so the correction term matters most), 1.01 for normal data with \(\kappa = 0.4\), and about 0.99, 0.95, and 0.94 for gamma data with \(\kappa\) = 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8; the ratio of the realized risk to the minimum risk was within about 0.03 of 1 in each case (its Monte Carlo standard error is about 0.01). When \(A/c\) is small and the population is strongly skewed the procedure stops early: the variance estimate rests on the third and fourth sample moments, which are very variable in small samples, and sampling ends the first time the criterion is met. For gamma data with \(\kappa = 1.3\) and \(c = 1\) the ratio of sample sizes was about 0.58, 0.74, 0.85, and 0.93 at \(A\) = 900, 9,000, 90,000, and 900,000 (0.86 and 0.94 for the last two in a second set of runs). Use seq_mr_cv_sensitivity to see the behavior for your own constants before collecting data.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

See also

seq_mr_cv_pilot for the pilot size and seq_mr_cv_sensitivity to study the procedure before collecting data; the accuracy in parameter estimation companion seq_aipe_cv; in DMAR, mr_cv (the same procedure with the published variance), the estimator cv, and the fixed sample size planner ss_aipe_cv.

Other seq_mr_cv: seq_mr_cv_pilot(), seq_mr_sensitivity

Examples

# The worked example of Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016, pp. 637-638): the
# number of age appropriate books in the homes of third graders. A home
# visit costs 75 dollars and A = 1000 / 0.05^2.
books <- c(36, 53, 19, 11, 10, 24, 14, 65, 18, 48, 25, 35, 13, 18, 3, 41,
           5, 3, 44, 26, 13, 39, 2, 3, 26, 22, 8, 15, 12, 22, 5, 21, 23,
           40, 18)
m <- seq_mr_cv_pilot(A = 400000, c = 75)
m
#> [1] 18

# After the pilot sample the rule is not met, so sampling continues.
seq_mr_cv(books[1:m], A = 400000, c = 75)
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 18
#>   Criterion n     : 36
#> 
#>   cv                : 0.7391157
#>   risk              : 5354.513
#>   xi_squared        : 0.1802031
#>   optimal_n         : 36
#>   current_n         : 18
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# With all 35 observations the default (corrected) variance asks for one
# more; the article's own variance reproduces its printed result (risk
# 4891.284, stop at 35).
seq_mr_cv(books, A = 400000, c = 75)
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 35
#>   Criterion n     : 36
#> 
#>   cv                : 0.7013904
#>   risk              : 4977.259
#>   xi_squared        : 0.2058226
#>   optimal_n         : 36
#>   current_n         : 35
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE
seq_mr_cv(books, A = 400000, c = 75, variance = "published")
#> Sequential check (minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation))
#> 
#>   Current n       : 35
#>   Criterion n     : 35
#> 
#>   cv                : 0.7013904
#>   risk              : 4891.284
#>   xi_squared        : 0.1982998
#>   optimal_n         : 35
#>   current_n         : 35
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
#> 
#>   Note: The variance estimate is Equation 22 of Chattopadhyay and
#>         Kelley (2016), as requested with variance = "published". It
#>         agrees with the default estimator for normal data and can
#>         differ otherwise; see ?seq_mr_cv.
